prompt: What forms when an alkyl halide, RX, reacts with magnesium metal in ether or THF?

choices.why: RH forms only if the Grignard reagent is later protonated, for example by water.
No oxygen is involved. Magnesium inserts to give RMgX, which has a carbon–magnesium bond.

choices.text: A coupled alkane, R–R, and MgX2
choices.why: Magnesium doesn't join two alkyl groups here; it gives RMgX, a Grignard reagent.

explanation: Alkyl halides react with magnesium metal in ether or tetrahydrofuran (THF) solvent to yield alkylmagnesium halides, RMgX. These products are called Grignard reagents after their discoverer, Victor Grignard.

prompt: In which solvents are Grignard reagents prepared?

choices.why: Water protonates and destroys Grignard reagents: RMgX + H2O → RH + HOMgX.
Acid, like water, supplies a proton that converts the Grignard reagent into R–H.
NH3 (pKa 35) is acidic enough to protonate a Grignard reagent, as Exercise 10.6.1 shows.

explanation: Alkyl halides react with magnesium metal in ether or tetrahydrofuran (THF) solvent to give Grignard reagents. Because the reagents are such strong bases, they must be kept away from water and other proton sources.

prompt: In what year did Victor Grignard receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry?
explanation: Grignard reagents are named after their discoverer, Francois Auguste Victor Grignard, who received the 1912 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

prompt: Why are Grignard reagents classified as organometallic compounds?

choices.text: They are made in an organic solvent
choices.why: The solvent doesn't define the class. Organometallic compounds contain a carbon–metal bond.
The C–X bond of the alkyl halide is gone. RMgX has a C–Mg bond, which makes it organometallic.

choices.text: They contain a metal ion with no bond to carbon
choices.why: The defining feature is a bond between carbon and the metal, here magnesium.

explanation: Grignard reagents (RMgX) are examples of organometallic compounds because they contain a carbon–metal bond, in this case a carbon–magnesium bond.

prompt: Which organohalides rarely react with magnesium?

choices.why: Chlorides do react, though they are less reactive than bromides and iodides.
Bromides react readily with magnesium to form Grignard reagents.
Iodides react readily with magnesium to form Grignard reagents.

explanation: The halogen can be Cl, Br or I, although chlorides are less reactive than bromides and iodides. Organofluorides rarely react with magnesium.

prompt: From which kinds of organohalide can Grignard reagents be made?

choices.text: Alkyl halides only, not vinylic or aryl halides
choices.why: Grignard reagents can also be made from alkenyl (vinylic) and aryl (aromatic) halides.

choices.text: Aryl halides only, not alkyl halides
choices.why: Alkyl and alkenyl (vinylic) halides work too.

choices.text: Primary alkyl halides only, not secondary or tertiary
choices.why: Primary, secondary and tertiary alkyl halides all work, as do vinylic and aryl halides.

explanation: In addition to alkyl halides (primary, secondary or tertiary), Grignard reagents can be made from alkenyl (vinylic) and aryl (aromatic) halides.

prompt: In a Grignard reagent, what is the character of the carbon atom bonded to magnesium?

choices.text: Electron-poor and electrophilic, like the carbon of an alkyl halide
choices.why: The C–Mg bond is polarized the other way from C–X: the carbon is electron-rich, shown red in the electrostatic potential map.

choices.text: Neutral, because the C–Mg bond is nonpolar
choices.why: The carbon–magnesium bond is polarized, making the carbon electron-rich.

choices.text: Acidic, able to give up a proton
choices.why: The carbon is strongly basic; it takes protons from water and other acids.

explanation: The carbon–magnesium bond is polarized, making the carbon atom of a Grignard reagent both nucleophilic and basic. An electrostatic potential map of methylmagnesium iodide shows the electron-rich (red) character of the carbon bonded to magnesium.

prompt: A Grignard reagent is formally the magnesium salt of a carbon acid, R3C–H. What does that make its carbon group?

choices.why: The carbon is the electron-rich end of the C–Mg bond; it is an anion, not a cation.
The carbon has an electron pair in its bond to magnesium, not a single unpaired electron.
The carbon is nucleophilic and basic, as a carbanion should be.

explanation: A Grignard reagent is formally the magnesium salt, R3C^− ^+MgX, of a carbon acid, R3C–H, and is thus a carbon anion, or carbanion. Because hydrocarbons are such weak acids, carbanions are very strong bases.

prompt: What range of pKa values does the section give for hydrocarbons?

choices.why: Hydrocarbons are much weaker acids than that; their pKa values run from 44 to 60.
Hydrocarbons are weaker acids still. NH3, with pKa 35, is a stronger acid than a typical hydrocarbon.
Such values would make hydrocarbons fairly strong acids. Their pKa values are 44 to 60.

explanation: Hydrocarbons are such weak acids, with pKa's in the range 44 to 60, that their conjugate bases, carbon anions, are very strong bases. That is why Grignard reagents are destroyed by water.

prompt: Why must Grignard reagents be protected from atmospheric moisture?

choices.text: Water protonates them, giving R–H and destroying the reagent
Water converts them into alcohols, ROH, and magnesium salts
choices.why: Water acts as an acid: RMgX + H2O → RH + HOMgX. The carbon ends up bonded to H, not OH.

choices.text: Water turns them back into the alkyl halides, RX, they came from
choices.why: The halogen isn't put back on carbon. Water supplies a proton, giving R–H.

choices.text: Water dissolves the magnesium, so no reagent can form
choices.why: The problem is an acid–base reaction: the strongly basic carbon takes a proton from water.

explanation: Carbon anions are very strong bases, so Grignard reagents must be protected from atmospheric moisture to prevent their being protonated and destroyed in acid–base reactions: R–Mg–X + H2O → R–H + HO–Mg–X.

prompt: 1-Bromohexane reacts with Mg in ether, and the Grignard reagent formed is then treated with water. What is the organic product?

choices.why: Water protonates the carbon; it doesn't attach an OH group. The product is the alkane.
The bromine isn't put back. Water supplies a proton to the carbon that was bonded to magnesium.
Water doesn't join two hexyl groups together; it just supplies a proton.

explanation: 1-Bromohexane and Mg give hexylmagnesium bromide, whose strongly basic carbon takes a proton from water: the product is hexane, plus HOMgBr.

prompt: Which of these reactions should occur as written? (a) CH3MgBr + H–C≡C–H → CH4 + H–C≡C–MgBr, where acetylene's pKa is 25. (b) CH3MgBr + NH3 → CH4 + H2N–MgBr, where the pKa of NH3 is 35.

choices.why: NH3 (pKa 35) is also a far stronger acid than methane, so CH3MgBr removes a proton from it too.
Acetylene (pKa 25) is an even stronger acid than NH3, so it is deprotonated as well.
A Grignard reagent is a very strong base, the conjugate base of a hydrocarbon, so it deprotonates both of these much stronger acids.

explanation: A Grignard reagent behaves as a carbanion, and since hydrocarbons have pKa values of 44 to 60, carbanions are very strong bases. CH3MgBr is the conjugate base of methane, so it deprotonates both acetylene (pKa 25) and NH3 (pKa 35), giving CH4 each time (Exercise 10.6.1).

prompt: How could you replace the halogen of an alkyl halide, RX, with a deuterium atom?

choices.text: Make the Grignard reagent, RMgX, then add D2O
Make the Grignard reagent, RMgX, then add H2O
choices.why: Water would give R–H. D2O is needed to put deuterium on the carbon.

choices.text: Make the Grignard reagent in D2O instead of ether
choices.why: Grignard reagents are made in ether or THF and must be protected from water; D2O is added after the reagent forms.

choices.text: Treat RX with NBS and ultraviolet light
choices.why: NBS brominates allylic positions; it doesn't introduce deuterium.

explanation: A Grignard reagent reacts with water to give R–H, replacing the halogen by hydrogen. Using D2O instead puts a deuterium atom where the halogen was: RX → RMgX → R–D (Exercise 10.6.2).

prompt: What connection does the section draw between Grignard reagents and biological chemistry?

choices.text: They don't occur in organisms but model biological carbon nucleophiles
They occur widely in organisms as carbon nucleophiles
choices.why: Grignard reagents themselves don't occur in living organisms.

choices.text: They are the electrophiles enzymes use to form C–C bonds
choices.why: The carbon of a Grignard reagent is nucleophilic and basic, not electrophilic.

choices.text: They have nothing in common with any reactions in living organisms
choices.why: They act as a simple model for more complex carbon-based nucleophiles that are important in biological chemistry.

explanation: Grignard reagents don't occur in living organisms, but they serve as useful carbon-based nucleophiles in the laboratory and act as a simple model for the more complex carbon-based nucleophiles that are important in biological chemistry (Chapter 29).

prompt: Which reaction gives methylmagnesium iodide, CH3MgI?

choices.text: Iodomethane with magnesium metal in ether

choices.why: Grignard reagents are made from organohalides and magnesium metal. Methane has no halogen.

choices.text: Iodomethane with magnesium metal in water
choices.why: Water would protonate and destroy the Grignard reagent; it is made in ether or THF.

choices.text: Fluoromethane with magnesium metal in ether
choices.why: That couldn't give an iodide, and organofluorides rarely react with magnesium anyway.

explanation: Alkyl halides react with magnesium metal in ether or THF to give RMgX. Iodomethane and Mg in ether give methylmagnesium iodide, whose carbon is electron-rich: basic and nucleophilic.
